title: Power, Batteries and Charging

mentor.name: CELL-8
mentor.character: Asks for the units before the number, and refuses to accept an answer that does not carry them.

summary: You finish able to size a battery pack from a mission, add up every consumer on a robot, predict the voltage sag at peak current and say how long the machine really runs. You also build the charging, gauging and protection logic that keeps that pack alive for hundreds of cycles.

lessons.title: The Cellar Wakes
lessons.goal: Convert a load quoted in milliamps into the watts it takes off a rail.
lessons.theory:
Every part bolted to a robot is bought with three numbers: the **volts** its rail must supply, the **amps** it pulls from that rail, and the product of the two, the **watts** it burns. Volts alone say nothing about cost. Amps alone say nothing either.

Datasheets almost never quote amps. A Raspberry Pi 4 idles near `700 mA` on its 5 V rail, an RPLIDAR A1 pulls about `400 mA` while its head spins, an MG996R servo holding a load sits around `900 mA` on 6 V. Those are **milliamps**, one thousandth of an amp each. Drop them straight into a watt formula and the answer comes out a thousand times too big.

So the first rule of this cellar: convert, then multiply. Divide milliamps by `1000.0` to reach amps, then multiply by volts. The Pi lands at 5.0 times 0.7, which is `3.5 W`.

Every name you write here carries its unit in the name. `volts`, `milliamps`, `power_w`. A variable called `current` is a bug waiting to happen, because nobody reading it later knows which thousand it meant.
lessons.task: Write `power_w(volts, milliamps)` so it reaches amps before it multiplies by `volts`, and print the watts of every load in `LOADS`.
lessons.hint: One amp is a thousand milliamps, so `700.0 / 1000.0` is `0.7` and that is the number the multiplication wants.

lessons.title: The Hour Behind the Watt
lessons.goal: Turn watts and hours into watt hours, and watt hours back into hours.
lessons.theory:
A watt is a **rate**. A watt hour is an **amount**. Confusing the two is the most common mistake in a power review, and it always shows up as a runtime that is off by a factor of somebody guessed.

A robot that burns `12 W` and runs for `8 h` has spent `96 Wh`. Run the same sum backwards and a `96 Wh` pack feeding a `12 W` robot lasts 8 hours, while the same pack feeding a `40 W` robot lasts 2.4. Nothing about the pack changed, only the rate pulling on it.

That is why a pack is advertised in watt hours when the seller is honest, and why every energy budget in this course ends in watt hours before it ends in a decision.

The two functions you are about to write are the same equation. One multiplies, one divides, and knowing which one you need is most of the work.
lessons.task: Write `stored_wh(watts, hours)` and `hours_from(energy_wh, watts)` so each one is the other rearranged.

    # TODO: how much energy a load of this size spends in this time
    return 0.0


def hours_from(energy_wh, watts):
    # TODO: how long that much energy lasts at this load
    return 0.0

print("96 Wh at 12 W ->", round(hours_from(96.0, 12.0), 2), "h")
print("96 Wh at 40 W ->", round(hours_from(96.0, 40.0), 2), "h")

    return watts * hours

lessons.title: The Number on the Wrapper
lessons.goal: Convert a cell label in milliamp hours into energy in watt hours.
lessons.theory:
A cell is labelled in **milliamp hours**, and that number is not energy. It is charge: how many milliamps the cell can push for one hour. To turn charge into energy you have to know the voltage it comes out at.

A Samsung INR18650-35E is `3500 mAh` at `3.6 V` nominal. Divide by `1000.0` and you have `3.5 Ah`. Multiply by 3.6 and you have `12.6 Wh`. That last number is the one you can compare against a budget, because watt hours divided by watts gives hours and milliamp hours divided by watts gives nothing at all.

Watch the chemistry while you do it. A LiFePO4 cell at `3.2 V` nominal holding the same amp hours stores about eleven percent less energy than a lithium ion cell at 3.6, and no amount of staring at the amp hour figure will reveal that.

Name the variable for the unit it holds. `capacity_mah` is milliamp hours, `capacity_ah` is amp hours, `pack_wh` is energy. When those three share a name is when a design goes wrong by a factor of a thousand.
lessons.task: Write `pack_wh(capacity_mah, nominal_v)` returning the energy of one cell in watt hours, and print it for every cell in `CELLS`.
lessons.hint: Divide by `1000.0` into a `capacity_ah` of your own, then multiply that by the nominal volts.

lessons.title: Two Packs, One Answer
lessons.goal: Rank two packs by energy and show why the amp hour figure cannot rank them.
lessons.theory:
A shop lists a `5000 mAh` pack at 12 V and a `2500 mAh` pack at 24 V. The first number is twice the second, and the two packs hold exactly the same energy: 60 watt hours each. The bigger label sold nothing but volts you were not told about.

This is why sellers of small packs quote milliamp hours and sellers of large packs quote watt hours. The milliamp hour figure is bigger and it hides the voltage. As soon as two packs sit at different voltages, only watt hours can compare them.

There is one honest use for the amp hour figure: comparing two packs at the same voltage, where it is proportional to energy. The moment the voltages differ, convert first.

When you compare floats, never ask whether two are equal. Ask whether the difference is smaller than something you consider a tie, here `0.01` Wh, because `60.000000000000014` and `60.0` are the same pack.

lessons.starter:
def pack_wh(capacity_mah, nominal_v):
    return (capacity_mah / 1000.0) * nominal_v


def bigger_pack(a_mah, a_v, b_mah, b_v):
    # TODO: rank the two by energy, not by the label on the shrink wrap
    return "same"

print(bigger_pack(5000.0, 12.0, 5000.0, 7.4))
print(bigger_pack(2000.0, 11.1, 5200.0, 11.1))

lessons.title: The First Honest Guess
lessons.goal: Estimate runtime by dividing capacity by draw and name the three reasons it reads high.
lessons.theory:
Divide milliamp hours by milliamps and the milli cancels on both sides, leaving hours. A `3400 mAh` cell feeding a steady `850 mA` gives exactly 4 hours. That is the whole calculation, and it is the number every datasheet and every forum post quotes.

It is also a ceiling, never a prediction, for three reasons this course spends chapters on. You cannot empty a pack to zero without ruining it, so part of that capacity is off limits. The voltage sags under load, so the same watts cost more amps as the pack drains. And the draw is never one steady number, it is a robot that drives, stops, thinks and drives again.

A useful habit from today: when a number is an upper bound, say so in the name or in the print. `ceiling_h` invites a margin. `runtime_h` invites somebody to plan a mission around it.

Every estimate in this cellar gets more honest as the course goes on, and each correction is a multiplier below one applied to this first guess.

lessons.starter:
CAPACITY_MAH = 3400.0
DRAWS_MA = (850.0, 1200.0, 2000.0)


def runtime_h(capacity_mah, draw_ma):
    # TODO: the milli cancels, so this is one division
    return 0.0


for draw_ma in DRAWS_MA:
    print(draw_ma, "mA ->", round(runtime_h(CAPACITY_MAH, draw_ma), 2), "h ceiling")
lessons.hint: Both sides are in milli, so you can divide them directly and read the answer as hours.

lessons.title: Three Voltages, Never One
lessons.goal: State the nominal, full and empty voltage of a cell and compute the swing between them.
lessons.theory:
A cell does not have a voltage. It has a **window**, and it walks across that window as it empties. Lithium ion leaves the charger at `4.2 V` and is considered flat at `3.0 V`. LiFePO4 goes from `3.65 V` down to `2.5 V`. A NiMH cell runs `1.45 V` to `1.0 V`, and one lead acid cell `2.4 V` to `1.75 V`.

The **nominal** voltage is the third number, and it is a label, not a measurement. It is roughly where the cell spends most of its discharge, and it exists so that you can multiply it by amp hours and get an honest average energy. Lithium ion is quoted at `3.6 V` or `3.7 V` depending on who wrote the sheet, LiFePO4 at `3.2 V`.

That window is why nothing on a robot runs directly off the pack unless it can survive the whole range. A 3S lithium ion pack hands you anything from 12.6 down to 9.0 volts, and the electronics must not care which end of that it is seeing.

The swing matters when you choose a chemistry. LiFePO4 has a famously flat curve, which is pleasant for regulators and miserable for anyone trying to guess the charge left from the voltage alone.
lessons.task: Write `span_v(chemistry)` that reads the row out of `CHEMISTRY` and returns how far the cell falls from `full_v` to `empty_v`.
lessons.hint: The loop already shows you how to unpack a row of the table. Do the same inside the function with the argument it was given.

lessons.title: Cells in a Line
lessons.goal: Stack cells in series and scale the whole voltage window by the count.
lessons.theory:
Wire the positive of one cell to the negative of the next and the voltages add while the amp hours stay exactly where they were. Three lithium ion cells in series is a **3S** pack, and every point of the window multiplies by three: `10.8 V` nominal, `12.6 V` full, `9.0 V` empty.

This is the first decision in any pack design, because it sets whether your motors and your converters see a voltage they can use. A 4S pack at `14.4 V` nominal suits a 12 V motor rail with room for the sag. A 6S LiFePO4 pack lands at `19.2 V` nominal and never goes above `21.9 V`, which keeps a 24 V rated converter comfortably inside its limits.

What series does not give you is capacity. Three 3500 mAh cells in series is still a 3500 mAh pack. It holds three times the energy because energy is amp hours times volts, and it is the volts that grew.

Design against the **empty** end of the window, never the nominal. A converter that needs 10 V in will quit long before a 3S pack is actually flat.
lessons.task: Write `pack_window_v(cells_in_series, chemistry)` so the returned tuple scales all three of `nominal_v`, `full_v` and `empty_v`.
lessons.hint: The count multiplies each of the three volt figures, so the tuple you return has three products in it.

lessons.title: Cells Side by Side
lessons.goal: Stack cells in parallel and scale capacity and current limit while the voltage stays put.
lessons.theory:
Wire all the positives together and all the negatives together and you get a **parallel group**. The voltage window does not move at all. What grows is the amp hours and the current the group can deliver without cooking.

Two Samsung INR18650-35E cells in parallel is a `7000 mAh` group at the same `3.6 V` nominal, and where one cell was comfortable at `8 A` the pair is comfortable at `16 A`. Both numbers doubled because both are per cell numbers and there are now two cells sharing the work.

This is the usual answer to a robot that browns out under load. Adding a parallel cell does not raise the voltage, it lowers how hard each cell is being pushed, and a cell pushed less sags less, heats less and lasts more cycles.

Parallel cells must start at the same voltage before you join them. Two cells half a volt apart will dump enormous current into each other the moment the wire closes, and neither of them is protected against it.
lessons.task: Write `parallel_pack(cells_in_parallel, cell_capacity_mah, cell_max_a)` so it scales both numbers a parallel group owns.
lessons.hint: Both of the numbers the function receives are per cell numbers, so both of them scale with the count.

lessons.title: Three Up, Two Across
lessons.goal: Compute the voltage, capacity and energy of a pack described as SxP.
lessons.theory:
A pack is named by the two counts together. **3S2P** means three cells in series repeated twice in parallel: six cells, `10.8 V` nominal, `7000 mAh`, and `75.6 Wh` of energy.

The arithmetic has one rule and it is easy to get backwards. The series count owns the volts. The parallel count owns the amp hours. The energy needs both, because watt hours are amp hours times volts, and that is the number your budget will actually spend.

Notice what this buys you as a designer. If a robot needs more runtime you add parallel. If it needs a higher rail you add series. If it needs both you multiply cells fast, and a 6S4P pack of 18650 cells is twenty four cells, about 1.6 kg of them, and `302.4 Wh` that airlines have opinions about.

Be strict with the names. `pack_v` is volts, `pack_mah` is milliamp hours, `pack_wh` is energy, and the conversion by `1000.0` sits between the last two.
lessons.task: Write `pack_spec(series, parallel, cell_nominal_v, cell_capacity_mah)` filling in `pack_v`, `pack_mah` and `pack_wh`.
lessons.hint: Series owns the volts, parallel owns the milliamp hours, and the energy needs the amp hours, so divide before you multiply.

lessons.title: The Part You Never Spend
lessons.goal: Remove a reserve fraction from a pack and compare the honest runtime with the ceiling.
lessons.theory:
A lithium ion pack taken down to `3.0 V` per cell on every cycle will not see many cycles. Take the same pack to `3.5 V` per cell instead and it lasts several times longer, at the cost of leaving perhaps twenty percent of the energy in the pack.

That twenty percent is not waste, it is the **reserve**, and every serious robot has one. Some of it protects cycle life, some of it is the margin that lets the machine crawl back to the dock when the mission went long.

So a pack has two capacities: the one on the label and the one you are allowed to spend. Budgets, runtimes and mission plans use the second. `75.6 Wh` of pack with a `0.20` reserve is `60.48 Wh` of energy you may actually plan around.

The difference is not small. A 14 W robot on that pack goes from a 5.4 hour ceiling to a 4.32 hour plan, and the second number is the one that will still be true tomorrow.
lessons.task: Write `usable_wh(total_wh, reserve_fraction)` and then `honest_runtime_h(total_wh, reserve_fraction, draw_w)` on top of it, so the printed ceiling and the printed honest figure stop agreeing.

PACK_WH = 75.6
DRAW_W = 14.0

    return total_wh


def honest_runtime_h(total_wh, reserve_fraction, draw_w):

lessons.title: The Rate Called C
lessons.goal: Convert a C rate into amps using the capacity of the pack it refers to.
lessons.theory:
Cells are compared with a rate that carries no amps in it at all. **1C** is whatever current empties the pack in one hour, so on a `3.4 Ah` cell 1C is `3.4 A`, and on a `100 Ah` truck battery 1C is `100 A`.

The point of the notation is that it travels between sizes. Saying a chemistry handles 10C tells you something about the chemistry. Saying it handles 34 A tells you something about one particular cell.

The conversion has one trap and it is the one this whole course keeps circling. The C rate multiplies the capacity in **amp hours**. Multiply it by milliamp hours and you get milliamps, which is a thousand times off and looks perfectly reasonable on the screen.

Read it the other way too. A robot pulling `1.7 A` from a `3.4 Ah` pack is running at 0.5C, and that is a number you can compare against any datasheet in the drawer.
lessons.task: Write `current_from_c(c_rate, capacity_mah)` so it builds `capacity_ah` before it multiplies, and print the amps for every rate listed.
lessons.hint: Build `capacity_ah` on its own line first, so the multiplication is obviously in the right units.

lessons.title: What the Cell Will Not Give
lessons.goal: Compute a pack current limit from the per cell rating and judge a load against it.
lessons.theory:
Every cell has a **continuous discharge** rating, and pulling above it does not blow anything up on the spot. It heats the cell, and a hot cell ages fast. The damage is invisible until the pack that used to run four hours runs two.

A good design rule for ordinary 18650 cells is `2C` continuous, which on a `3500 mAh` cell is `7 A`. High drain cells go far above that, and the cheapest cells on the market quietly go below it whatever the wrapper claims.

Parallel cells raise the limit in proportion, because each of them carries its share. A 2P group of those cells is good for `14 A`, and the same load that was uncomfortable on one cell is relaxed on two.

Do not design to the edge of the rating. A load at ninety percent of the limit is legal and still wrong, because the sag, the heat and the cycle life all get worse long before the number is exceeded. Call that region what it is and leave it.

CAPACITY_MAH = 3500.0

    return 0.0


def verdict(load_a, limit_a):

    return "ok"

lessons.title: The Burst It Can Survive
lessons.goal: Judge a short high current pulse against both an amp limit and a time limit.
lessons.theory:
A drive motor that stalls against a table leg pulls four or five times its running current until something gives. A cell datasheet answers that case with a second rating: a **pulse** or burst current, valid for a stated number of seconds.

So a burst has two numbers and both of them can fail. `25 A` out of a pack rated `21 A` in pulse is over current no matter how brief. `18 A` for thirty seconds out of a pack rated `21 A` for ten seconds is inside the amp limit and still abuse, because the rating expired twenty seconds ago.

There is a third number nobody prints, the duty. A ten second pulse every fifteen seconds is not a burst, it is a continuous load with a fancy name, and the cell will treat it that way by getting hot.

When you write a check like this, test the harder failure first. Reporting `"too long"` for a current that was never allowed sends the next engineer looking in the wrong place.
lessons.task: Write `burst_verdict(burst_a, burst_s, burst_limit_a, burst_max_s)` returning `"over current"`, `"too long"` or `"ok"`, in that order of priority.

BURST_C = 6.0
CAPACITY_AH = 3.5
BURST_MAX_S = 10.0


def burst_verdict(burst_a, burst_s, burst_limit_a, burst_max_s):
    # TODO: two limits can fail, and one of them matters more
    return "ok"


burst_limit_a = BURST_C * CAPACITY_AH
for burst_a, burst_s in ((10.0, 2.0), (25.0, 2.0), (18.0, 30.0)):
    print(burst_a, "A for", burst_s, "s of", round(burst_limit_a, 1), "A ->",

lessons.title: The Weight of the Energy
lessons.goal: Estimate pack mass from energy and chemistry, including the overhead around the cells.
lessons.theory:
Energy has a mass, and on anything that moves you pay for it twice: once to carry it and once to accelerate it. The figure that matters is **energy density** in watt hours per kilogram.

At cell level, lithium ion 18650 cells land near `250 Wh/kg`, LiFePO4 near `120`, NiMH near `90`, and lead acid near `35`. That last number is why a lead acid robot is a heavy robot, and why lead acid survives anyway in machines where the mass is ballast you wanted regardless.

Cells are not a pack. Holders, nickel strip, wiring, a BMS board, fuses and a case add mass that carries no energy at all. A factor of `1.35` on cell mass is a fair first estimate for a small robot pack, and it gets worse the smaller the pack is.

The same `200 Wh` mission is about `1.08 kg` of lithium ion pack and about `7.71 kg` of lead acid pack. Nothing else about the design changed.
lessons.task: Write `pack_mass_kg(energy_wh, chemistry)` using `DENSITY_WH_PER_KG` for the cells and `PACK_OVERHEAD` for everything strapped around them.
lessons.hint: Divide the energy by the density to get the mass of the cells into a `cell_kg`, then apply the overhead factor to it.

lessons.title: The Ledger Opens
lessons.goal: Add a table of consumers into a single figure in watts.
lessons.theory:
A power budget is a table, and the discipline is that nothing on the robot is allowed to be missing from it. Every board, every motor, every sensor, every indicator LED gets a line with the rail it sits on and the current it pulls.

The rails differ, so the currents cannot be added. Two hundred milliamps at 3.3 V and two hundred milliamps at 12 V are not the same load and summing them gives a number with no meaning. Convert each line to **watts** first and the addition becomes legal, because watts are watts wherever they came from.

Use the numbers people actually measure. A Jetson Orin Nano under a vision load sits near `3000 mA` on its 5 V input, an RPLIDAR A1 near `400 mA`, a pair of small gearmotors near `900 mA` on 12 V. Later chapters will correct these for duty cycle and for converter losses, and the correction only works if the table was complete in the first place.

The first version of every budget is wrong by whatever somebody forgot. Write the loop so adding a line is one line of data, never one line of code.

lessons.title: Nothing Runs All the Time
lessons.goal: Turn on and off times into a duty cycle and an average current.
lessons.theory:
The headlight bar on a delivery robot pulls `1200 mA`, and it is on for two seconds out of every twenty. Budgeting it at 1200 mA sizes the pack for a robot that does not exist.

The **duty cycle** is the fraction of the time a load is actually drawing. Two seconds on and eighteen off is `0.1`, and the average current is the peak multiplied by that fraction: `120 mA`. The peak has not gone away, it still decides the wire and the converter, but the pack only ever sees the average.

Duty is where most of the honesty in a budget lives. A gripper servo that grabs for a second and a half every half minute is `0.05`, which turns a 900 mA part into a 45 mA part. Get the duty wrong in the optimistic direction and every runtime you promise afterwards is fiction.

Measure it, do not guess it. A duty is two timings: how long the thing runs and how long it waits, and both are things you can watch on a real robot with a stopwatch.
lessons.task: Write `duty_from(on_s, off_s)` and `average_ma(peak_ma, duty)`, then let the loop print the duty and the average for every load in `PROFILE`.

    ("RPLIDAR A1", 400.0, 55.0, 5.0),
    ("gripper servo", 900.0, 1.5, 28.5),
)

    # TODO: the fraction of the whole period the load is really drawing
    return 1.0


def average_ma(peak_ma, duty):
    # TODO: the pack only sees the average
    return peak_ma


for name, peak_ma, on_s, off_s in PROFILE:
    duty = duty_from(on_s, off_s)
    print(name, "duty", round(duty, 3), "->", round(average_ma(peak_ma, duty), 1), "mA")

lessons.title: The Worst Second
lessons.goal: Compute the peak and the average of the same budget and say which one sizes what.
lessons.theory:
A budget produces two totals and confusing them ruins hardware in both directions.

The **average** is what the pack has to store. It is every line multiplied by its duty, and it decides how many amp hours you buy. The **peak** is every line at once with no duty at all, and it decides the wire gauge, the fuse, the connector and the converter rating. Nothing in the robot may be sized on the wrong one of these.

On the table in front of you the average is about `24 W` and the peak is about `58 W`. Size the pack for 58 and you carry more than twice the mass you need. Size the 12 V converter for 24 and it shuts down the first time the headlights and both motors are on together.

The honest peak is the worst combination that can actually happen at the same instant, not the arithmetic sum of everything on the sheet. If the gripper never closes while the robot drives, that pair does not belong in the same peak. Say which combinations are real before you add them up.
lessons.task: Write `average_w(budget)` and `peak_w(budget)`, one with the duty applied and one without, and print both plus their ratio.

lessons.title: The Robot in the Drawer
lessons.goal: Add up a standby budget and compute how long the pack survives with the robot switched off.
lessons.theory:
A robot that is off is not drawing zero. The BMS is watching the cells, the microcontroller is in stop mode waiting for a button, the radio is in deep sleep, and somebody left a status LED on.

Those numbers are tiny and the time is enormous, which is exactly the combination that empties packs. A `0.06 mA` BMS is nothing. An `8 mA` status LED is also nothing, until you multiply it by three weeks in a cupboard and find a pack sitting below its safe voltage with no way back.

This is the budget nobody writes down, and it is the one that decides whether a machine that sat over a holiday still works in January.

lessons.title: The Mission Has Phases
lessons.goal: Weight a budget by the minutes each phase lasts and find the true average watts.
lessons.theory:
A duty cycle per part is the small version of this idea. The large version is that a robot has **phases**, and each one has its own power and its own length.

A delivery run might be two hours idle at the dock at `6 W`, twelve minutes driving at `34 W`, twenty five minutes scanning shelves at `22 W`, and twelve minutes driving back. The energy of each phase is its watts multiplied by its hours, and the mission energy is the sum.

The average that comes out of that is not the average of the four numbers. It is the total energy divided by the total time, which weights each phase by how long it actually lasted. Here it lands near `12 W`, far below the `34 W` phase that dominates the intuition and nowhere near the average of the column.

Size the pack on this number and add a reserve. Size it on the driving phase and you have bought a pack twice as heavy as the robot needed, which slows it down, which makes the driving phase cost more.

lessons.title: From Watts to the Shopping List
lessons.goal: Convert an average power and a target runtime into the amp hours a pack must hold.
lessons.theory:
A budget in watts does not buy anything. Cells are sold in amp hours at a voltage, so the last step of any budget is a conversion the other way.

It has three parts and they go in this order. Multiply the average watts by the hours you want and you have the **energy** the mission needs. Divide by the usable fraction, because the reserve is not yours to spend. Divide by the pack voltage, because that is what turns watt hours into amp hours.

A `12.34 W` robot for eight hours needs `98.7 Wh`. With a `0.8` usable fraction that is `123.4 Wh` of pack, and on a 3S lithium ion pack at `10.8 V` nominal that is `11.43 Ah`. Four `3500 mAh` cells in parallel gets you there, so the pack is 3S4P and twelve cells.

Divide by the wrong voltage and the answer is wrong in the most expensive direction. Use the nominal voltage of the pack, not the full one, because full is where the pack spends the least of its life.

lessons.title: The Margin You Design In
lessons.goal: Apply an unknowns margin and an ageing margin to a budget and judge two pack sizes against it.
lessons.theory:
The budget you just built is a best case built from datasheet numbers, and datasheet numbers are measured by people who wanted a good number.

Two margins cover most of the gap. The **unknowns** margin, around twenty percent, covers the loads you forgot, the converter losses you have not modelled yet and the parts that draw more than the sheet says. The **ageing** margin, around ten percent, covers the fact that the pack in two years holds less than the pack today.

They multiply rather than add, because each one applies to the result of the last. A `12.34 W` budget with `0.2` and `0.1` becomes `16.29 W`, and a mission that looked like it fitted a 75.6 Wh pack now does not.

A margin is not pessimism, it is the difference between a design that ships and a design that gets a second pack strapped to it with cable ties. Put it in the code, print it, and let the verdict be a word rather than a feeling.

A budget that is only a total tells you whether the design fits. A budget that is **ranked** tells you what to do about it when it does not.

The **mission energy** is the design figure multiplied by the hours you promised. Writing it as one function matters more than it looks. A budget that lives in four scripts and a spreadsheet drifts apart within a week, and the version that ends up in the robot is whichever one somebody had open.

From here the course starts taking the number apart again. Sag, converter efficiency and temperature all push it up, and every one of them is a correction to this same sheet.

lessons.title: The Cell Pushes Back
lessons.goal: Compute the terminal voltage of a cell under load from its internal resistance.
lessons.theory:
A cell is not a voltage source. It is a voltage source with a resistor welded inside it, and that resistor is the reason a robot browns out the instant the motors start.

The number is called **internal resistance** and it is quoted in milliohms. A healthy 18650 sits somewhere near `40 mohm` when new and warm. The terminal voltage you can actually measure is the open circuit voltage minus the current multiplied by that resistance, and nothing you do to the wiring changes it.

Pull `1 A` through 40 milliohms and you lose `0.04 V`, which nobody notices. Pull `10 A` and you lose `0.4 V`, which is most of the distance between a full lithium ion cell and a half empty one. The pack did not lose charge, it lost voltage, and the two look identical to anything measuring the rail.

Watch the units once more. Milliohms divided by `1000.0` are ohms, and only ohms may be multiplied by amps to get volts. This is the same thousand as the milliamps, and it catches people just as often.

lessons.title: Resistance Stacks Too
lessons.goal: Compute pack internal resistance from the series and parallel counts and see the sag shrink.
lessons.theory:
Internal resistance follows the stack exactly the way you would expect from any other resistor. Series **adds** it, parallel **divides** it, and a pack of `40 mohm` cells arranged 3S1P is a `120 mohm` pack.

That is the hidden cost of a tall pack. Every cell you add in series raises the voltage, which is what you wanted, and raises the resistance, which you did not ask for. The sag under a given current grows with the same count that grew the voltage.

Parallel is the cure. A 3S2P pack of the same cells is `60 mohm` and a 3S4P is `30 mohm`. At `10 A` those three packs sag `1.2 V`, `0.6 V` and `0.3 V` from the same starting point, and only the last one keeps a 12 V motor rail comfortable.

This is why the answer to a robot that resets when it accelerates is often more cells rather than better wiring. The wiring is usually not where the resistance lives.

The internal resistance of the pack on your bench is not the one in the datasheet. It depends on the cells, the welds, the age and the temperature, so you measure it.

Two points are enough. Read the terminal voltage at a light load and again at a heavy one. The resistance is the **change in volts divided by the change in amps**, and multiplying by `1000.0` puts it back into milliohms.

Measure `11.62 V` at `0.5 A` and `11.17 V` at `8.0 A` and you have 0.45 volts over 7.5 amps, which is 0.06 ohms, which is `60 mohm`. That is a 3S2P pack of ordinary cells and the number is believable, which is the other half of the test: a measurement of 4 milliohms or 400 means you measured something else.

The same two points give you the open circuit voltage for free. Take the light load reading and add back the sag it already had, and you have the voltage the pack would show with nothing connected, without waiting for it to rest.

lessons.title: The Floor Under the Rail
lessons.goal: Predict whether a peak current drives the pack below the brownout floor at each state of charge.
lessons.theory:
A robot that reboots when it accelerates is not a software problem. The peak current sagged the pack below what the converters needed, they dropped their rails, and the computer that was mid sentence stopped existing.

The test is arithmetic and you can do it before you build anything. Take the open circuit voltage at the state of charge you care about, subtract the sag at the **peak** current, and compare against the floor: the lowest input voltage every converter on the robot still works at.

What makes it interesting is that the answer changes as the pack drains. A 3S pack at `12.4 V` open circuit survives a `25 A` peak through `60 mohm` with `10.9 V` left. The same peak at `10.5 V` open circuit leaves `9.0 V`, and if the floor is `9.5 V` the robot dies at that moment, not when the pack is empty.

So the real end of a discharge is not the cell cutoff. It is the first state of charge where a legitimate peak puts the rail under the floor, and it always arrives earlier than the datasheet suggests.

lessons.title: The Resistance You Soldered In
lessons.goal: Add cable and connector resistance to the pack and see what share of the sag they own.
lessons.theory:
The pack is not the only resistor between the cells and the motors. The wire is one, and so is every connector, every fuse holder and every switch on the way.

Copper is quoted in milliohms per metre: `13.17` for 16 AWG, `8.28` for 14 AWG, `5.21` for 12 AWG. The number that matters is the **round trip**, because the current goes out on one wire and comes back on the other, so a 0.6 metre run of 16 AWG is 1.2 metres of copper and about `15.8 mohm`.

Connectors are worse than people expect for how small they are. An XT60 pair is around `0.5 mohm` when new and clean, and a tired one is several times that. Two of them on a run add another milliohm to the path.

Against a `60 mohm` pack that wiring is about a quarter of the total, which is exactly the kind of thing that turns a design that passed on paper into a robot that browns out. Add the path to the pack before you check the floor.

lessons.title: The Energy That Never Leaves
lessons.goal: Compute the internal heating loss at a current and its share of the power delivered.
lessons.theory:
The volts lost to internal resistance do not disappear, they become heat inside the pack. The power spent that way is the current **squared** times the resistance, and the square is what makes it a design problem rather than a footnote.

At `5 A` through `60 mohm` the pack heats itself with `1.5 W`, which a taped brick of 18650 cells shrugs off. At `25 A` the same pack is making `37.5 W`, which is a soldering iron sitting inside your robot, and it will be doing that every time the machine accelerates.

Two consequences follow. The energy is gone from the mission, so a pack worked hard delivers fewer watt hours than the same pack worked gently. And the heat raises the cell temperature, which changes the resistance, which changes the heat.

Always report it as a share. One and a half watts of loss against fifty five delivered is under three percent and nobody cares. Thirty seven against two hundred and fifty is fifteen percent, and that is a pack that will be warm to the touch and short of its label.

lessons.title: The Gauge That Panics
lessons.goal: Compensate a loaded voltage reading back to open circuit before judging the pack.

A robot reads `10.4 V` at its pack terminals while both motors pull `20 A`. If the low battery threshold is `10.6 V` the machine parks itself and reports an empty pack that is in fact two thirds full.

The fix is to compensate before you judge: add the current multiplied by the resistance back onto the measurement, and compare **that** against the resting threshold. It costs one multiplication and it is the difference between a robot that finishes its route and one that stops halfway.

Compensation needs an honest resistance, which is why you measured it two lessons ago, and it needs the current at the moment of the reading. A gauge that reads volts without reading amps cannot do this, and it will keep panicking.

lessons.title: Cold Makes It Worse
lessons.goal: Scale internal resistance by temperature and recompute the sag at each one.
lessons.theory:
Internal resistance is a chemistry rate, and chemistry slows down in the cold. A lithium ion cell that measures `60 mohm` as a pack at 25 degrees measures well over twice that near twenty below.

The usual shape, good enough for a budget, is a multiplier on the warm value: about `1.0` at 25 degrees, `1.6` at zero, `2.3` at minus ten, `3.5` at minus twenty. Cells differ, but the direction never does.

What that does to a robot is dramatic. The same `20 A` peak that cost `1.2 V` of sag in a warm workshop costs `2.76 V` at minus ten, and the rail that had margin does not any more. This is why outdoor machines brown out on the first cold morning after a winter of working fine indoors.

There is a warm side to the story. The pack heats itself while it works, so the resistance falls during the first minutes of a mission and the sag improves. Design for the cold start, not for the cell you measured after an hour of driving.

lessons.title: One Dip Is Not Empty
lessons.goal: Trip a low voltage cutoff only after the loaded rail stays down for several samples.
lessons.theory:
A pack under a heavy pulse dips below the cutoff and climbs straight back the moment the pulse ends. A controller that trips on the first sample will park a robot with a third of its energy left, every single time it accelerates near the end of a run.

A controller that never trips is worse, because a lithium cell dragged below its floor is damaged and does not tell you.

The standard answer is to require the condition to **persist**. Count consecutive samples below the floor and only act when the count reaches a threshold, three in this loop, and reset the count the instant a sample comes back. That is one integer of state and it removes an entire class of false alarms.

The same pattern reappears in every protection in this course, so learn its shape here: a condition, a counter called `under`, a threshold, and a reset on any good sample.

lessons.title: The Linear Rail Pays Full Price
lessons.goal: Show that a linear regulator draws the load current from the pack whatever the voltage drop is.
lessons.theory:
A linear regulator is a valve. The current that leaves it is the current that entered it, and the extra volts it did not pass on are burned. That second half is the famous one. The first half is the one that decides your runtime.

A 5 V rail delivering `1 A` from an `11.1 V` pack pulls exactly `1 A` off the pack. The pack is handing over `11.1 W` so the load can receive `5 W`, and the difference is heat. The efficiency of the arrangement is simply the ratio of the two voltages, `45` percent here, and no clever layout improves it.

What surprises people is the direction it moves. Charge the pack to `12.6 V` and the efficiency falls to just under `40` percent, because the regulator now has more volts to throw away for the same delivered watts. A linear rail is worst when the pack is fullest.

The heat side of this you can size on a bench with a multimeter. The side that matters here is the amp hours: on a battery, a linear rail is a decision about runtime long before it is a decision about a heatsink.

lessons.title: The Switching Rail Buys the Ratio
lessons.goal: Compute pack current for a buck converter, where power is conserved instead of current.
lessons.theory:
A switching converter does not pass current through, it passes **power** through. What comes out is what went in minus a loss, so the input current is set by the voltage ratio rather than by the load current.

The arithmetic is three steps. The rail power is its volts times its amps. The pack power is that divided by the efficiency, because the loss is a fraction of the whole. The pack current is the pack power divided by the pack voltage.

The same 5 V rail at `1 A` from an `11.1 V` pack, through a buck at `0.92` efficiency, draws `0.49 A`. The linear regulator drew `1.0 A` for the identical load. That is half the pack current for the same robot, and it is the single biggest lever in this chapter.

Note which way the numbers move. Because power is conserved, a buck feeding a low rail from a high pack draws **less** current than it delivers, and the ratio grows as the pack voltage rises. The linear regulator gets worse with a full pack, the buck barely notices.

lessons.title: Efficiency Is Not a Number
lessons.goal: Interpolate a converter efficiency from a load table instead of using one headline figure.
lessons.theory:
The `94` percent on the front page of a converter datasheet is measured at one load, usually the one that flatters the part. Efficiency is a **curve**, and the ends of it are where robots live.

A typical small buck runs `0.72` at 50 milliamps, `0.88` at a quarter of an amp, `0.92` at half, `0.94` at one amp and back down to `0.91` at two. The dip at the bottom is switching and quiescent losses that do not shrink with the load, and it is why a big converter feeding a sleeping robot is so wasteful.

So a budget that uses one efficiency figure for both the driving phase and the idle phase is wrong in both. Look the number up at the load you actually have.

Between two points in the table you interpolate: work out how far along you are between them, and mix the two efficiencies in that proportion. That is the same straight line trick that will map voltage to charge in the next chapter, so it is worth writing once properly.

lessons.title: The Day the Rail Gives Up

Every regulator needs its output plus some headroom at the input, and below that it stops regulating. That headroom is the **dropout** voltage, and it decides when your pack is empty far more often than the cells do.

An old LM7805 wants about `2.0 V` of it, so a 5 V rail needs `7.0 V` at the input. A modern low dropout part wants `0.35 V` and needs `5.35 V`. A buck typically wants half a volt or so of margin above its output.

On a 2S lithium ion pack the window runs `8.4 V` down to `6.0 V`. The LM7805 quits at 7.0, which is `58` percent of the way through, and the rest of the pack is unreachable. The low dropout part and the buck never hit their limit inside that window at all.

So the question is never whether a regulator works. It is how much of your pack it lets you spend, and that is a number you can print.

A boost converter makes a rail higher than the pack. Power still crosses it, so making volts out of nothing means taking **more amps in than it gives out**.

lessons.title: Choose It by the Hours
lessons.goal: Compare a linear and a switching rail by the runtime each one leaves on the same pack.
lessons.theory:
The usual way to choose between a linear regulator and a switcher is heat: work out the watts burned and decide whether you can get rid of them. On a machine that plugs into a wall that is the whole question.

On a battery it is the wrong question, or at least the second one. The right question is **how many hours the robot runs**, and it is answered with the same two formulas you already have: the linear takes the pack voltage times the load current, the switcher takes the rail watts divided by its efficiency.

The linear regulator still wins somewhere: tiny loads, quiet analogue rails, and any rail whose voltage is close to the pack. Choose it on purpose, with the hours printed next to it, not because it was one part instead of six.

lessons.title: The Rail That Starves First
lessons.goal: Find which converter loses regulation first and recompute the real empty voltage of the pack.
lessons.theory:
A pack is empty when the robot stops working, and that is almost never when the cells are flat. It is when the **first** converter on the tree runs out of input voltage.

Take three pack fed rails: a 5 V buck that works down to `5.5 V`, a 12 V boost that gives up under `8.0 V`, and a motor driver with an undervoltage lockout at `9.6 V`. The cells are happy to `9.0 V`, but the driver quits at 9.6 and the robot is a paperweight from that moment on.

So the real window of this design is `12.6 V` down to `9.6 V`, which is `83` percent of the window you thought you had bought. The last seventeen percent exists, it is in the cells, and nothing on the robot can reach it.

The fix is a design decision, not a firmware one: raise the cell count, lower the lockout by choosing another driver, or accept the number and put it in the gauge so the robot calls itself empty at 9.6 and not at 9.0.

lessons.title: The Curve That Tells the Truth
lessons.goal: Map a rested cell voltage to a state of charge by interpolating an open circuit table.
lessons.theory:
A rested lithium ion cell has a repeatable relationship between its voltage and how full it is. That relationship is a **curve**, not a line, and it is the cheapest fuel gauge in existence.

The shape matters. From `4.20 V` down to about `3.68 V` the cell has spent sixty percent of its charge and the voltage has moved half a volt, which is easy to read. Below `3.45 V` the last tenth disappears in a cliff, and above 4.1 the curve is nearly flat. Two hundredths of a volt of measurement error near the top is worth ten percent of charge.

The table in this lesson is pairs of volts and charge for one cell at rest. To read a voltage that falls between two rows you interpolate, exactly as you did with the efficiency curve, which is the same straight line between two known points.

One cell, always. A pack voltage divided by the cell count is only the same thing if the cells are balanced, and the last lesson of this chapter is about what happens when they are not.

lessons.title: Wait Before You Believe It
lessons.goal: Model voltage relaxation after a load and show the charge reading climbing to the truth.
lessons.theory:
The open circuit table is only valid for a cell that is **at rest**, and a cell does not rest the instant the load goes away. It climbs back over minutes as the chemistry inside settles.

A reasonable model is an exponential recovery with a time constant of a couple of minutes. A cell sitting at `3.66 V` under load, whose true open circuit is `3.90 V`, has recovered about two thirds of the gap after `120 s` and almost all of it after `600 s`.

Read the table at the wrong moment and the answer is wrong in a specific direction: always **low**, sometimes by a third of the pack. A robot that checks its charge the second it stops will report a scare that resolves itself while nobody is looking.

This is the practical objection to voltage gauges, and the reason the next lessons count coulombs instead. A robot that never rests long enough to read its own curve needs another way to know.

lessons.title: Counting What Leaves
lessons.goal: Integrate current over time into milliamp hours spent and a remaining state of charge.
lessons.theory:
The other way to know how full a pack is does not look at voltage at all. It measures the current and adds it up. That is **coulomb counting**, and it is what every serious fuel gauge chip does.

The arithmetic is one line and the units are the whole difficulty. Amps multiplied by seconds are coulombs, but nobody buys cells in coulombs, so divide the seconds by `3600.0` to get hours and multiply by `1000.0` to land in the milliamp hours the label uses.

One amp for one minute is `16.67 mAh`. Ten amps for five minutes is `833 mAh`, which is a real bite out of a 7000 mAh pack and the kind of number a robot should be watching while it drives.

Coulomb counting has no opinion about sag, temperature or rest, which is its great advantage. Its weakness is that it only measures **change**, so it has to be told where it started, and any error it makes it keeps.

lessons.title: The Error That Accumulates
lessons.goal: Show a small current sense bias growing into a large charge error over hours.
lessons.theory:
A coulomb counter adds up its own mistakes. If the current sense reads two percent high, then every hour it invents two percent of an hour of current, and nothing ever takes it back.

Two percent sounds harmless. On a robot averaging `3 A` it is `60 mA` of imaginary current, which after eight hours is `480 mAh`, which on a 7000 mAh pack is nearly seven percent of the gauge. The robot thinks it is emptier than it is, or fuller, depending on which way the sense resistor is off.

The error is **unbounded** and that is the whole problem. A voltage gauge is noisy but it never drifts, because the curve does not move. A coulomb counter is quiet and precise and slowly walks away from reality.

So the two methods fail in opposite ways, which is exactly why the next lesson uses both.

lessons.title: Anchor It When It Rests
lessons.goal: Count coulombs while the robot works and snap the estimate to the voltage curve when it rests.
lessons.theory:
The two gauges have opposite faults, so the standard answer is to use both. Count coulombs continuously, because that is accurate over minutes, and **re anchor** to the open circuit curve whenever the robot has been still long enough for the reading to mean something.

The condition has two halves and both are needed: the current has to be under an idle threshold, and it has to have been under it for long enough to relax. A robot that stops for two seconds at a door has not rested.

Watch what the anchor does in this run. The counter starts from a wrong assumption of eighty percent, drifts along happily, and the first anchor drops it to where the cells actually are. The second anchor, later in the run, barely moves it, because from the first correction onwards the count was starting from the truth.

That is the shape of every practical fuel gauge: a fast estimator that drifts, corrected occasionally by a slow one that does not.

lessons.title: The Pack Is Not Its Label
lessons.goal: Apply cycle fade to the nameplate capacity and show the gauge error it causes.
lessons.theory:
A pack loses capacity as it is used. A reasonable figure for good lithium ion cells worked gently is about **three percent per hundred cycles**, and it is worse if the pack is run hot, charged to the very top, or emptied to the very bottom.

After five hundred cycles, roughly a year and a half of daily use, a `7000 mAh` pack is a `5950 mAh` pack. Everything downstream of that number is wrong by fifteen percent if nobody told the gauge.

That error is not symmetric in consequence. A gauge using the nameplate reports a charge that is too high, so the robot promises a runtime it cannot deliver and finds out at the far end of the building.

Real fuel gauge chips learn the number by watching full discharges. A simple robot can do something cruder and honest: store the cycle count, apply the fade, and print the capacity it is actually working with.

lessons.title: How Long Have I Got
lessons.goal: Turn a state of charge and a present draw into remaining hours above the reserve.
lessons.theory:
A percentage on a screen is not an answer. The question a robot has to answer is how many minutes of work are left, and that needs three numbers: the charge, the capacity and the current it is drawing right now.

The subtlety is the **reserve**. A robot at thirty percent with a twenty percent reserve does not have thirty percent of runtime left, it has ten. Subtract the reserve before you divide, or the machine will confidently drive itself into the floor of its own protection.

Below the reserve the honest answer is zero, not a negative number. A gauge that reports minus four minutes has told you nothing except that somebody forgot a guard.

Use the present draw, not the average one. A robot that is about to climb a ramp has minutes left, not hours, and the number should say so and then recover when the ramp is over.

The reserve is a blunt instrument. A robot two metres from its dock and a robot at the far end of a warehouse need very different amounts of energy held back, and a fixed twenty percent is wrong for both.

The sharp version computes the **return cost** from where the robot actually is. Distance divided by speed gives the seconds, seconds times the driving watts gives the energy, and that is what must stay in the pack. Two hundred and twenty metres at `0.6 m/s` drawing `34 W` costs about `3.5 Wh`.

Add a margin on top, because the way back may include the door that was closed and the corridor that was blocked. Twenty five percent of the return cost is cheap insurance and still far less than a flat pack reserve.

The decision this produces is one of the few a robot must make on its own, and it should be a word: carry on, or turn back now.

lessons.title: The Weakest Cell Decides
lessons.goal: Judge a pack on its lowest cell rather than on the average and show the two disagreeing.
lessons.theory:
A pack voltage is a sum, and a sum hides everything. Three cells at `3.55`, `3.52` and `3.10` volts average `3.39`, which looks like a pack with charge left. The third cell is nearly flat and it is the one that will be damaged.

Series cells all carry the same current, so when the weak one reaches its floor the pack is finished no matter what the other two have left. Discharging past that point pushes the weak cell into deep discharge, which damages it further, which makes it weaker still.

So every protection decision in a pack is made on the **minimum** cell, never on the average and never on the total. A monitor that only sees the pack terminal voltage cannot make that decision at all, which is the entire reason cell taps exist.

Print both numbers side by side once and the point makes itself. The average says carry on. The minimum says stop, and the minimum is right.

lessons.title: Two Phases and a Full Stop
lessons.goal: Classify a charging cell into constant current, constant voltage or finished.
lessons.theory:
A lithium cell is charged in two phases and then left alone, and mixing them up is how packs catch fire.

In **constant current** the charger pushes a fixed current and lets the cell voltage climb wherever it wants. This lasts from empty up to the moment the cell reaches its maximum voltage, `4.20 V` for ordinary lithium ion, and it delivers roughly the first eighty percent of the charge.

In **constant voltage** the charger holds exactly that voltage and the current falls away on its own, because the gap driving it is closing. The phase ends when the current has dropped to a **termination** threshold, usually somewhere near a twentieth of the capacity.

Then it stops. It does not trickle, it does not top up, it does not sit there holding `4.20 V` for a week. A lithium cell held at full voltage ages fast, which is why the third answer in this function is a full stop and not a third phase.

Charging has its own C rate and it is not the discharge one. Most lithium ion cells accept `0.5C` comfortably, many accept `1C`, and almost none should be charged faster than that without a datasheet in front of you saying so.

That calculation is the honest part of a charge time estimate. It scales exactly as you would expect: double the current and it halves.

The reason charge times do not halve in practice is the second phase, which is coming in two lessons and does not care how brave you were with the current.

lessons.title: The Long Tail
lessons.goal: Model the constant voltage taper and compute how long it runs before termination.
lessons.theory:
Once the cell reaches its ceiling voltage the charger stops pushing and starts holding. The current then falls away roughly **exponentially**, because what drives it is the shrinking difference between the charger and the cell.

A simple model with a time constant of about `25` minutes matches a small pack well enough to plan with. Starting from `3.5 A`, the current is down to a third of that in twenty five minutes and to a tenth in an hour.

So the last twenty percent of the charge takes about as long as the first sixty. That is not a defect, it is the shape of the chemistry, and any charger that claims otherwise either terminated early or was not charging a lithium cell.

lessons.title: Why Faster Is Not Twice as Fast
lessons.goal: Add both charging phases and show that doubling the current barely shortens the total.
lessons.theory:
Put the two phases together and something uncomfortable appears. The constant current phase halves when you double the current, exactly as promised. The constant voltage phase gets **longer**, because it starts from a higher current and has further to fall.

At `0.5C` this pack spends `1.2 h` pushing and about `0.96 h` tapering, for `2.16 h` in total. At `1C` it spends `0.6 h` pushing and about `1.25 h` tapering, for `1.85 h`. Twice the charge current bought fourteen percent of the time.

Meanwhile the fast charge heated the cells more, aged them faster and needed a supply twice the size. That trade is sometimes worth making, on a fleet that must turn around between shifts, and it is almost never worth making by default.

The model here is deliberately simple, one time constant for the taper regardless of the rate. It gets the shape and the lesson right, which is what a budget needs.
lessons.task: Write `charge_time_h(capacity_ah, start_soc, cc_end_soc, c_rate, tau_min, term_a)` returning `cc_h`, `cv_h` and their sum.

import math

CAPACITY_AH = 7.0
START_SOC = 0.2
CC_END_SOC = 0.8
TAU_MIN = 25.0
TERM_A = 0.35


def charge_time_h(capacity_ah, start_soc, cc_end_soc, c_rate, tau_min, term_a):
    charge_a = c_rate * capacity_ah
    cc_h = ((cc_end_soc - start_soc) * capacity_ah) / charge_a
    cv_h = (tau_min * math.log(charge_a / term_a)) / 60.0
    return (cc_h, cv_h, cc_h + cv_h)


for c_rate in (0.5, 1.0):

    print(c_rate, "C ->", round(cc_h, 2), "h push +", round(cv_h, 2), "h taper =",
          round(total_h, 2), "h")

lessons.title: What the Wall Pays
lessons.goal: Compute the energy drawn from the mains for one charge, including both efficiency losses.
lessons.theory:
The energy that leaves the wall is more than the energy that ends up in the pack, and it is lost in two places.

The cells themselves are not perfectly efficient. Nearly every electron you push in comes back out, but the voltage on the way in is higher than the voltage on the way out, so the **energy** efficiency of a lithium cell is around `0.94`. The rest became heat during the charge.

The charger loses its own share, typically `0.88` for an ordinary mains adapter and its converter. Multiply the two and about `83` percent of what leaves the socket arrives as usable energy.

So a `75.6 Wh` pack costs about `91 Wh` at the wall per full charge. Over five hundred cycles that is `45.7 kWh`, which is the number an operations manager will want and which nobody ever computes at design time.

lessons.title: Too Cold to Fill
lessons.goal: Return the charge rate a cell temperature allows, including the temperatures that allow none.
lessons.theory:
A lithium ion cell must not be charged below **zero degrees**. Not slowly, not gently: the lithium plates out as metal on the anode instead of intercalating, the damage is permanent, and enough of it makes an internal short.

Discharging in the cold is merely inefficient. Charging in the cold is destructive, and that asymmetry surprises people every winter.

Between zero and about ten degrees a reduced rate around `0.1C` is acceptable for most cells. From ten to forty five the normal rate applies. Above forty five, charging stops again, this time because heat and full cells together accelerate ageing and, far enough up, run away.

So the answer this function returns is a rate and a reason, because a robot that refuses to charge must be able to say which of the two walls it hit. The reasons here are `plating`, `cold`, `normal` and `hot`.
lessons.task: Write `charge_limit(temp_c, normal_c)` returning `(0.0, "plating")` under zero, `(0.1, "cold")` under ten, the normal rate with `"normal"`, and `(0.0, "hot")` above forty five.
lessons.hint: Take the bands in order from the coldest, and let the normal rate be the fallthrough at the end.

lessons.title: The Shelf Eats It Too
lessons.goal: Estimate calendar ageing from the charge level a pack is stored at.
lessons.theory:
A pack sitting in a cupboard loses capacity even though nobody used it. This is **calendar ageing**, it is separate from cycle wear, and the charge level it is stored at changes it by a factor of five.

The rough figures at room temperature: a pack stored full loses around twenty percent of its capacity in a year, a pack at sixty percent about eight, and a pack near forty percent about four. Heat multiplies all of them.

That is why a good charger for a robot that will sit over a holiday charges to storage level rather than to full, and why a spare pack in a drawer should never have been left on the charger.

The practical rule fits in one line: charge to full for work, store at about forty percent, and never leave a lithium pack sitting at `4.20 V` per cell for months.

lessons.hint: Look the storage level up in the table and scale it by the share of a year that `months` represents.

lessons.title: Sizing the Thing on the Wall
lessons.goal: Compute the supply power a charger needs at full pack voltage and pick a standard size.
lessons.theory:
The charger supply is sized at the **worst** moment, which is the end of the constant current phase: the current is still at its maximum and the pack voltage is nearly at its maximum too.

For a 4S pack that means `16.8 V`, not the `14.4 V` nominal that a careless calculation would use. At `3.5 A` that is `58.8 W` leaving the charger, and dividing by an efficiency of `0.88` gives about `67 W` coming in.

Then you buy a real part, and real parts come in sizes. Add headroom, twenty percent is sensible, and pick the first standard size above the answer. Running a supply at its rated limit continuously is how supplies become warm, then noisy, then dead.

Under sizing here has a specific and confusing symptom: the charge starts fine and stalls partway through, because the supply hits its limit exactly when the pack voltage rose enough to need the extra watts.

lessons.title: A Dock for Twenty Robots
lessons.goal: Work out how many robots a shared supply can charge at once and how long a fleet rotation takes.
lessons.theory:
One robot is a power budget. A fleet is a **schedule**, and the constraint moves from the pack to the building.

A charging room with a `600 W` supply and robots that need `67 W` each can run eight of them at once, not nine, because the remainder is not a slot. Twenty robots therefore need three rotations, and at `2.16 h` each that is `6.5 h` of night.

That fits an eight hour shift. Thirty robots would need four rotations and `8.6 h`, which does not, and the answer is either a bigger supply, a faster charge rate with all the ageing that carries, or accepting that part of the fleet starts the day partly charged.

Notice the shape of the arithmetic. Slots round **down**, because you cannot half connect a robot. Rotations round **up**, because a leftover robot still needs a full turn.

lessons.title: What the Guardian Watches
lessons.goal: Compare the sum of the cell taps against the measured pack voltage to detect a broken sense wire.
lessons.theory:
A battery management system exists because a pack terminal voltage tells you almost nothing. What it watches is **every cell separately**, through a set of thin sense wires called taps, plus the current through the pack and the temperature of the cells.

Those taps are the most fragile thing in the whole assembly. They are thin, they run past everything that vibrates, and when one breaks the BMS starts protecting a pack it can no longer see. A dead tap usually reads as a cell at zero or a cell at the rail, and either one produces a confident wrong decision.

The cheap test is arithmetic. Add the cells and compare against the pack voltage measured at the terminals. They should agree to within a small tolerance, a few hundredths of a volt for measurement noise, and if they do not then the wiring is lying rather than the pack.

Run that check before you trust any of the protections in this chapter, because every one of them is built on numbers that come through those wires.

lessons.hint: Compare the two numbers with an absolute difference, never with equality, because two measurements of the same thing never match exactly.

lessons.title: The Two Walls
lessons.goal: Classify one cell against its undervoltage and overvoltage limits.
lessons.theory:
Every cell has two hard limits and crossing either one damages it permanently.

The **undervoltage** wall for lithium ion is around `2.50 V`, and a protection cutoff is normally set above it, at `3.00 V` or higher, so the pack stops with margin rather than at the edge. Below the wall the copper current collector starts to dissolve, and a cell that has been there is not safe to charge again even if it appears to work.

The **overvoltage** wall is `4.25 V` for most lithium ion, with cutoffs set at `4.20` or `4.25`. Above it the cell is being pushed into a state where it makes heat faster than it can lose it.

A BMS applies both to each cell independently, which is the whole point of the taps. The scan in this lesson walks the pack and reports the first cell in trouble along with which wall it hit, because those two faults need different responses: one stops the load, the other stops the charger.

lessons.title: The Cells Drift Apart
lessons.goal: Measure cell spread in millivolts and classify how urgent the imbalance is.
lessons.theory:
Cells in series start matched and slowly stop being matched. Small differences in self discharge and internal resistance accumulate, and after a few hundred cycles the pack has a leader and a straggler.

The measure is the **spread**: the highest cell minus the lowest, reported in millivolts because the interesting range is small. Under `30 mV` a pack is healthy. Up to `100 mV` it is worth watching. Beyond that the pack is losing usable capacity, because the charge stops when the highest cell is full and the discharge stops when the lowest cell is empty.

A growing spread is also a diagnosis. A single cell that keeps falling behind is usually a cell with a higher self discharge, and it will keep getting worse. A whole pack that drifts evenly is usually a balancing circuit that is not doing its job.

Report it in millivolts and print it every cycle. It is the single most useful number about the health of a series pack.

lessons.title: Bleeding the Leader Down
lessons.goal: Compute passive balancing current and the hours it takes to remove an imbalance.
lessons.theory:
The common cure for imbalance is embarrassingly crude. A resistor is switched across the cell that is ahead and the excess charge is turned into heat until the others catch up. That is **passive balancing**, and almost every small BMS does it that way.

The current is Ohm's law and nothing more: a cell at `4.10 V` across a `33 ohm` bleed resistor pushes about `124 mA`. That is all the balancer has to work with, because a bigger current means a resistor that gets too hot to sit on a small board.

So the time is long. An imbalance of `150 mAh`, which is a couple of percent of a 7 Ah pack, takes over an hour of bleeding. A pack that arrives badly out of balance may need several charges to come together.

This is why balancing happens at the top of the charge, where the cell voltages spread out enough to tell which one is ahead, and why leaving a robot on the dock a while longer after it says it is full is not a waste of time.

lessons.title: How Long May It Be Wrong
lessons.goal: Apply an inverse time overcurrent curve so brief peaks ride through and sustained ones trip.
lessons.theory:
An overcurrent protection with a single threshold is useless on a robot. Motors draw several times their running current every time they start, and a BMS that trips on that never lets the machine move.

The answer is a **trip curve**: the further over the limit you are, the less time you are allowed to stay there. At `1.5` times the limit a pack will accept ten seconds. At twice the limit, two seconds. At three times, two tenths of a second, which is fast enough to protect the wiring from a genuine short.

Below the first row of the curve nothing trips at all, which is deliberate. A load ten percent over the continuous rating is a thermal question for another part of the system, not an emergency.

Read the curve from the bottom up and keep the last row you passed. That way a current that clears several rows ends up with the tightest time, which is the one that matters.

lessons.hint: One guard inside the loop. Because the rows are in order, the last one that matches is automatically the tightest.

lessons.title: The Part That Is Meant to Die
lessons.goal: Size a fuse from the derated continuous current and check a burst against its energy rating.
lessons.theory:
A fuse is the last protection and the only one with no software in it. Sizing it has two halves and people usually do only the first.

The first half is the continuous current. A fuse does not carry its printed rating forever in a warm enclosure, so **derate** it, typically to seventy five percent. A `12 A` continuous load therefore wants a fuse rated at least `16 A`, and you buy the next standard size up.

The second half is whether the fuse survives the bursts that are supposed to be normal. Fuses are characterised by their melting energy, the current squared multiplied by the time, written I squared t. A `60 A` inrush lasting two tenths of a second is `720` amp squared seconds, and if the fuse you chose is rated below that it will blow on a healthy start.

A fuse that blows during normal operation is worse than no fuse, because somebody will replace it with a bigger one, and the bigger one was never sized for anything.

lessons.title: Two Windows, Not One
lessons.goal: Apply separate temperature limits for charging and discharging to the same cell reading.
lessons.theory:
A pack has two temperature windows and they are not the same size, which is the single most common mistake in a homemade BMS.

**Discharging** is allowed from about minus twenty to sixty degrees. Cold discharge is inefficient and sags badly, but it does not destroy anything.

**Charging** is allowed only from zero to about forty five. Below zero the plating problem makes the damage permanent, above forty five the ageing accelerates sharply.

So the same cell at minus five degrees is perfectly free to drive the robot home and must not accept a single milliamp from the charger. A robot that comes in from a cold yard should drive to the dock, sit there warming up, and start charging when it is ready, and the only way to build that behaviour is to ask the temperature question with the mode in your hand.

lessons.title: Closing the Switch Gently
lessons.goal: Compute inrush current into bulk capacitance and size a precharge resistor and its delay.
lessons.theory:
Close a contactor between a pack and a robot full of bulk capacitors and, for an instant, the capacitors are a short circuit. The only thing limiting the current is the resistance of the path.

An `11.1 V` pack through `20 mohm` of wiring and contacts delivers `555 A` into that capacitance. It lasts microseconds, it welds contactor contacts together, it pits connectors, and it is why big packs do not simply switch on.

The fix is a **precharge**: a resistor in parallel with the main switch that fills the capacitors slowly first. A `22 ohm` resistor limits the same event to about `0.5 A`, and the bank of `4700 uF` is charged to within a few percent after three time constants, about `0.31 s`. Then the main contactor closes with almost no voltage across it and nothing happens at all.

Size the resistor for the delay you can tolerate and check the heat it takes during that moment. It is brief, but it is not nothing.

lessons.title: A Fault That Stays Faulted
lessons.goal: Latch a protection fault and re-arm it only after a deliberate clear and enough clean samples.
lessons.theory:
A protection that clears itself the moment the condition goes away is not a protection, it is an oscillator. The overcurrent trips, the load disappears, the current falls, the protection re arms, the load comes back, and the pack is now being switched on and off several times a second.

So faults **latch**. Once tripped, the state stays tripped until two separate things are true: the condition has been clear for long enough to believe it, and somebody or something has explicitly asked for a reset.

Watch the run in this lesson at the fifth sample. The fault has just tripped, an operator asks for a clear one sample later, and the machine refuses because it has not seen enough clean samples yet. The request is not queued and not remembered. That is correct behaviour, and building it any other way is how a pack ends up being re armed into a short circuit.

This pattern, a latch plus a counted clear condition plus an explicit request, is the shape of every safety state machine you will ever write.

lessons.title: Pulling Harder Gets You Less
lessons.goal: Apply the Peukert relationship to find the usable capacity at a draw above the rated one.
lessons.theory:
A pack rated `100 Ah` is rated at a particular current, usually a very gentle one. Pull harder and you do not get 100 amp hours, you get fewer, and the effect has a name: **Peukert**.

The rule of thumb is a power law with an exponent that depends on the chemistry. Lead acid is around `1.25` and it is brutal: a 100 Ah battery rated at `5 A` delivers about `71 Ah` at 20 amps and `56 Ah` at fifty. Lithium ion is around `1.05` and barely notices, delivering `93 Ah` at the same twenty amps.

That difference is one of the strongest arguments for lithium on a robot. The lead pack is not just heavier, it is heavier **and** it shrinks exactly when the machine is working hardest.

The correction goes on top of everything else in this course, not instead of it. Sag, reserve, temperature and Peukert all bite at once, and all of them bite hardest during the drive phase.

lessons.title: Run It Until It Stops
lessons.goal: Step a repeating mission profile until the usable energy is gone and count the missions completed.
lessons.theory:
Every runtime figure so far has been a division. That is fine for a robot with one steady load and useless for a robot with a **schedule**.

The honest way is to step the profile. Spend the energy of each phase, add its hours, and stop when the usable energy is gone. What comes out is not an average, it is the number of complete missions the pack supports, and that is the number an operations plan is written from.

On this profile a mission is twenty minutes and costs about `5.47 Wh`. A `60.48 Wh` usable pack therefore delivers eleven complete missions and dies partway through the twelfth. Eleven is the answer. Eleven and a half is not a thing a delivery robot can do.

The pattern also lets you ask better questions later. What if the scan phase were shorter, what if the idle draw halved. Both are one edit to the table rather than a new formula.

lessons.title: The Cold Keeps Some of It
lessons.goal: Derate usable capacity by temperature and recompute the runtime at each one.
lessons.theory:
Cold does two separate things to a pack and this course has now met both. It raises the internal resistance, which is the sag, and it lowers the **usable capacity**, which is the runtime.

The second effect is roughly this: about `85` percent of the nameplate at zero degrees, `75` at minus ten, `60` at minus twenty. The energy has not been destroyed, it is temporarily unreachable, and it comes back when the pack warms up.

For a robot that means a winter morning shift is not a shorter version of a summer one, it is a different plan. A machine that ran eleven missions in a warm building runs six or seven outdoors at minus ten, and no amount of firmware fixes that.

What does help is heating the pack, which costs energy but buys back more than it spends, and insulating the enclosure so the heat the cells make while working stays where it is useful.

lessons.title: The Cost of a Deep Cycle
lessons.goal: Compare cycle life at several depths of discharge and cost the energy the pack delivers over its life.
lessons.theory:
How long a pack lasts is decided less by how many cycles you run than by how **deep** they are. A lithium ion pack cycled to empty every day gives around `500` cycles. Cycled to eighty percent depth it gives about `900`, to sixty about `1500`, to forty about `3000`.

That looks like an argument for shallow cycles until you notice each cycle delivers less energy. The number that settles it is the **total energy over the life of the pack**: cycles multiplied by the depth multiplied by the pack energy.

Run the numbers on a `75.6 Wh` pack that costs eighty units. At full depth it delivers `37.8 kWh` over its life, which is `2.12` per kWh. At sixty percent depth it delivers `68 kWh`, which is `1.18`. The shallow cycling pack is nearly twice as cheap per unit of work.

So the reserve you have been carrying since the first chapter is not just insurance. It is the cheapest maintenance decision available, and it pays in the accounts rather than in the specification.

lessons.title: What a Mission Really Costs
lessons.goal: Add the electricity and the pack wear of one mission and see which of the two dominates.
lessons.theory:
A robot mission costs money in two ways and almost everybody counts only the first.

The **electricity** is the energy taken from the wall, which is the mission energy inflated by the cell and charger losses. At a quarter of a unit per kilowatt hour, a `34.77 Wh` mission costs about one cent. Nobody is going to plan around that.

The **pack wear** is the share of the pack you spent doing it, priced at the cost per kilowatt hour from the previous lesson. At `1.18` per kWh delivered, that same mission costs about four cents of pack.

The battery therefore costs four times as much as the electricity that fills it, which reverses the intuition most people arrive with. It also changes what is worth optimising: shaving watts off a rail saves both, but running shallower cycles only touches the larger of the two.

lessons.title: Buy the Pack for Its Last Day
lessons.goal: Size a pack so the mission still fits when the cells have faded to their end of life capacity.
lessons.theory:
A pack that exactly meets the mission on the day it is unwrapped fails the mission a year later. Cells are normally considered worn out at **eighty percent** of nameplate, and that is a fully working pack, not a broken one.

So the sizing has three divisions stacked on one multiplication. Take the mission energy, add the margin, then divide by the usable fraction because of the reserve and by the end of life fraction because of the fade.

A `100 Wh` daily requirement with a twenty percent margin, a `0.8` usable fraction and a `0.8` end of life fraction needs `187.5 Wh` of pack. That is nearly twice the naive answer, and it is the reason experienced people quote pack sizes that look generous.

The alternative is a fleet that works beautifully for six months and then starts failing its last delivery of the day, which is the most expensive way to discover this arithmetic.

lessons.title: The Pack You Have to Carry
lessons.goal: Show that runtime grows more slowly than pack size because the extra mass costs power to move.
lessons.theory:
Doubling the pack does not double the runtime on anything that moves, because the robot now has to carry the pack it just bought.

Model it simply. The machine has a base draw that does not depend on mass, the computer and the sensors, and a driving term that grows with mass, roughly `4 W` per kilogram for a small indoor robot on flat floors. Pack level energy density around `185 Wh/kg` turns watt hours into kilograms.

The result is diminishing returns you can print. Going from `75.6 Wh` to `151.2 Wh` takes the runtime from `2.8 h` to `5.2 h`, not `5.6`. Doubling again reaches `9.1 h` rather than `11.2`. Each doubling delivers less than the last.

Somewhere past that the curve flattens completely and a bigger pack buys nothing, which is why aircraft have an endurance limit no battery chemistry has yet argued with. Print the hours per watt hour and watch the number fall.
