lessons.title: How Hot Does It Get
lessons.goal: Turn internal heating into a steady state pack temperature and judge it against the safe limit.
lessons.theory:
The internal heating from chapter three has to go somewhere, and where it goes is the temperature of the cells. In steady state the rise above ambient is the loss in watts multiplied by the **thermal resistance** of the pack to its surroundings.

A small taped brick of cells with no airflow is around `1.8` degrees per watt. At `5 A` through `60 mohm` the loss is `1.5 W` and the pack sits under three degrees above ambient, which is nothing. At `15 A` the loss is `13.5 W` and the pack settles near `49` degrees in a warm room. At `25 A` the arithmetic says ninety, which is a number you should never reach because something else should have stopped it first.

The limits worth marking are `45` degrees, where charging must stop and ageing accelerates, and `60`, where a lithium pack is in real trouble.

Thermal resistance is the cheapest thing to improve in the whole design. Spacing the cells, adding a fan or bonding the pack to a metal plate can halve it, and it halves the rise for every current at once.

lessons.goal: Classify a pack against the transport thresholds using its energy in watt hours.
lessons.theory:
The last thing a pack design has to survive is a shipping desk, and the only number anybody there cares about is **watt hours**. Not cells, not amp hours, not chemistry beyond the word lithium.

The thresholds worth knowing for passenger air travel are `100 Wh` and `160 Wh`. Under a hundred, a spare pack travels in cabin baggage with no fuss. Between a hundred and a hundred and sixty it needs airline approval and there is normally a limit of two. Above a hundred and sixty it is cargo only, under dangerous goods rules, with paperwork and a trained shipper.

The packs from this course fall on both sides of both lines. The 3S2P pack is `75.6 Wh` and travels freely. Doubling it puts you at `151.2 Wh` and into the approval band. The big 6S4P pack at `302.4 Wh` cannot fly with a passenger at all.

This is a design constraint, not an afterthought. If the robot has to be carried to a customer site, the pack size was decided by a regulation before it was decided by a mission.

The customer gave you watts per phase. The robot has parts, and the parts do not know what a phase is. The bridge between the two is a table where every consumer carries a **duty per phase**, and it is the single most useful document in a power design.

Multiply, sum by column, and you have the design power of each phase. Compare it with what was promised and you get the only answer that matters: how much headroom each phase has, and whether any of them is already over before a single part has been bought.

When a phase comes out over budget, this table is also where you fix it. The duty of one consumer in one phase is one number to change, and its effect on the whole design is a rerun rather than a rewrite.

lessons.title: The Tree Under the Robot
lessons.goal: Compute the pack current of the full rail tree including every converter quiescent draw.
lessons.theory:
The robot has three rails. The motors run from a `12 V` buck, the compute and the lidar from a `5 V` buck, and the analogue sensors from a `3.3 V` linear regulator that exists to keep switching noise out of them.

The tree turns rail watts into pack amps, each rail by its own rule, and this time the quiescent current of each converter is on the sheet as well. Fifteen milliamps twice is nothing next to four amps of motors, and it is most of the standby draw when the robot is parked.

Run it at two pack voltages: the `14.4 V` nominal and the `14.0 V` reserve floor where the robot is supposed to stop. The current is higher at the lower voltage, because the buck converters keep their output constant and take what they need.

That number, the pack current at the reserve floor with everything running, is the one the next three lessons all depend on. It sizes the sag, the fuse and the heat.

lessons.title: The Worst Instant of the Route
lessons.goal: Sag the pack at peak current and check every rail input against its own minimum.
lessons.theory:
Now the parts of this course come together. The pack is `80 mohm` because 4S2P doubles and halves a `40 mohm` cell, the wiring and connectors add `17 mohm`, and at peak the tree pulls a little over four amps through all of it.

Run it from the reserve floor, `14.0 V` open circuit, and the terminals sit near `13.6 V`. Every rail needs less than that, so every rail keeps regulating and the robot works.

Now run it from a genuinely flat pack at `12.0 V`, which is where the cells would stop you rather than the reserve. The terminals fall under `11.7 V`, the 12 V buck needs `12.5 V`, and the motors stop. Not the computer, not the sensors: the motors, on a robot that is presumably in the middle of a corridor.

That is the strongest argument for the reserve in the whole course. It is not about cycle life here, it is about the fact that the rails die before the cells do, and stopping at 14.0 volts is what keeps the machine drivable to the end.
lessons.task: Write `terminal_v(ocv_v, current_a, pack_mohm, wiring_mohm)` and `rail_check(rails, terminal)` returning the first starved rail or `("all rails", "fed")`.
lessons.hint: Add the two resistances before you convert them to ohms, and let the rail loop return the moment it finds one that is short.

lessons.title: The Gauge on the Handlebar
lessons.goal: Report charge, usable energy, deliveries left and the return decision from the cell voltages.
lessons.theory:
The gauge on this robot answers one question in four numbers, and it makes every one of them from the **lowest** cell rather than the pack.

The charge comes from the open circuit curve. The usable energy is that charge with the reserve taken off, multiplied by the pack energy. The deliveries left is the usable energy divided by the cost of one delivery, rounded down, because there is no such thing as most of a delivery. The last number is the decision: whether what is left still covers the trip back to the dock.

Watch the third case in the run. Three cells read comfortably and one has fallen to `3.30 V`, so the charge is near nine percent, which is under the reserve, so there is nothing left to spend and the answer is to return now. The pack terminal voltage in that state would have looked entirely reasonable.

That is the gauge finished: cheap to compute, honest about the reserve, and impossible to fool with an average.
lessons.task: Write `gauge(cell_volts, pack_wh, reserve, mission_wh, return_wh)` producing `soc` from the lowest cell, the usable energy, `missions_left` with `int`, and the decision.
lessons.hint: Four lines in order: the curve on the worst cell, the reserve taken off and clamped at zero, the whole deliveries, and the guard that turns the robot around.

lessons.title: The Layer That Says No
lessons.goal: Combine the cell, temperature and current protections into one ordered verdict.
lessons.theory:
The protections have been written one at a time and now they have to answer as one voice, in a fixed order, with the most dangerous condition first.

Cell voltage comes first, because a cell outside its window is being damaged right now. Temperature is next, and it depends on the mode, since the same five degrees below zero is fine for driving and forbidden for charging. Current is last, because the trip curve already gave brief peaks their allowance.

The function returns the **first** fault it finds and nothing else. A protection layer that returns a list of everything wrong is a debugging tool, not a safety device, and the machine acting on it has to pick one thing to do anyway.

And when nothing is wrong it answers `armed`, which is a deliberate word. It does not mean fine, it means the layer is watching and has found no reason to intervene.
lessons.task: Write `protect(cell_volts, temp_c, current_a, mode)` returning `"cell undervoltage"`, `"cell overvoltage"`, `"temperature"`, `"overcurrent"` or `"armed"`, in that order.
lessons.hint: Four guards, each returning immediately, and `window_ok` is already written so the temperature test is one comparison against its answer.

lessons.title: The Cellar Signs It Off
lessons.goal: Judge every number the design produced against its limit and print one verdict for the machine.
lessons.theory:
A power review ends with a sheet, and every line of it is a number this chapter produced next to the limit it had to respect.

The route needs `96.25 Wh` and the pack holds `100.8`. At the reserve floor and full peak the terminals sit at `13.61 V` and the hungriest rail needs `12.5`. The peak pack current is `4.07 A` against a `14 A` continuous limit. The pack settles a couple of degrees above ambient. The fuse is a `7.5 A` part against a derated need of `5.43`.

The half that people get wrong is the **direction**. Some of these have to be at least the limit and some at most, and a checker that applies one rule to both passes designs that will burn. That is why each row carries its own mode.

One note goes on the sheet without failing it: at `100.8 Wh` this pack is over the hundred watt hour line, so it flies only with airline approval. That was decided the moment the route asked for ninety six watt hours, and it is worth knowing before somebody promises to carry the robot to a customer.
lessons.task: Write `judge(have, need, mode)` for both `"at least"` and `"at most"` rows, then let the loop print each line and the final verdict.

    ("pack temperature at peak", 27.4, 45.0, "C", "at most"),
    ("fuse rating", 7.5, 5.43, "A", "at least"),
    ("transport, cargo threshold", 100.8, 160.0, "Wh", "at most"),
)


def judge(have, need, mode):
    # TODO: the mode decides which way the comparison points
    return have > need


failed = 0
for name, have, need, unit, mode in CHECKS:
    good = judge(have, need, mode)
    if not good:
        failed = failed + 1
    print(name + ":", have, unit, mode, need, unit, "->", "pass" if good else "FAIL")
